shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita (current US$)
shots.narration: In 2012, the average Japanese produced about forty-nine and a half thousand dollars a year. The average Spaniard, about twenty-eight and a half. {p} Japan was almost seventy-five percent richer. And Spain was in the middle of a brutal crisis: one in four Spaniards who wanted a job couldn't find one. {pp} In 2024, Spain passed Japan. In 2025, it pulled further ahead: about thirty-eight and a half thousand dollars per person, against thirty-six. {p} In more than sixty years of World Bank records, that had never happened before. {p} And Spain isn't alone. Italy passed Japan again in 2022. South Korea, for the first time, in 2023.

Japan: the bullet trains, the robots, and companies everyone knows, like Toyota, Sony and Nintendo. {p} Spain: one of Europe's biggest tourist destinations, a housing crash that left entire towns of empty apartments, and for years, Europe's worst unemployment. {p} Thirteen years later, the ranking is the other way around. How did that flip? {pp} There are two reasons. <soft>Only one of them is about Spain.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · official exchange rate, yen per US$ (period average)
shots.narration: The first reason is the yen. Japan didn't do anything dramatic. Its currency did. {p} In 2012, one dollar bought about eighty yen. In 2024, about a hundred and fifty. {p} The yen lost almost half its value against the dollar. {p} So a Japanese paycheck that never changed in yen was suddenly worth almost half as much in dollars. A salary of five million yen was worth about sixty-three thousand dollars in 2012. In 2024, about thirty-three thousand. {pp} Japan's economy, measured in dollars, shrank by about thirty percent between 2012 and 2025.

shots.src: Bank of Japan (negative rate from Feb 2016; ended 19 Mar 2024) · US Federal Reserve (target 5.25–5.50%, Jul 2023–Sep 2024)
shots.title: Why the yen fell
shots.narration: Why? Interest rates. {p} To fight decades of falling prices, the Bank of Japan kept its main rate below zero from 2016 until March 2024. {p} Meanwhile, America's central bank pushed its rate above five percent. {p} Investors sold yen to buy dollars that paid far more. The Bank of Japan only raised rates in 2024, its first hike in seventeen years. {p} And a weaker yen was partly the point: it makes Japanese exports cheaper, and Japan a bargain for tourists. {pp} Measured in yen, Japan didn't get poorer. Output per person, after inflation, grew about eleven percent since 2013.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · unemployment, total (% of labor force, modeled ILO estimate) · ESM financial assistance to Spain (2012): €41.3 bn
shots.narration: But that's only half the story. The other half is Spain. {p} In 2013, twenty-six percent of Spain's workforce was unemployed. Among young people, more than half. {p} The housing bubble had burst, and the banks needed a European rescue: about forty-one billion euros in loans, to keep them standing. {pp} By 2025, unemployment was about ten percent. Still the highest in the European Union, but the lowest in Spain in almost twenty years.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$), change since 2013 · OICA vehicle production 2024
shots.narration: Since then, Spain's output per person, after inflation, has grown about twenty-one percent. The eurozone's, about sixteen. Japan's, about eleven. {p} And lately, Spain has been sprinting. {p} In 2024 and 2025, it grew faster than Germany, France and Italy, and faster than the United States. In 2024, about three and a half percent, more than three times the eurozone's pace. {p} Its car factories, mostly foreign-owned, now build more vehicles than any country in Europe except Germany.

shots.title: Population change
shots.narration: And Spain has something Japan doesn't: more people. {p} Since 2019, thanks to immigration, Spain's population has grown by more than two million. Many come from Latin America, and already speak the language. {p} Japan's has shrunk by more than three million. {pp} Since its peak in 2010, Japan has lost about four point seven million people, more than the entire population of Croatia.
Quick favor: if you're enjoying this, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} Now, what is Spain actually selling? {pp} Mostly, sunshine. Quite literally.

shots.src: INE Frontur (3 Feb 2026): 96.8 million international tourists in Spain, 2025 · JNTO (Jan 2026): 42.7 million visitors to Japan, 2025 · INE tourism satellite account (12.6% of GDP, 2024) · Red Eléctrica (55.5% renewable electricity, 2025)
shots.title: International tourists, 2025
shots.narration: In 2025, Spain welcomed almost ninety-seven million foreign tourists, a new record. Only France gets more. {p} Japan had a record year too: almost forty-three million. {pp} Spain, with about forty percent of Japan's population, received more than twice as many visitors. {p} Tourism brings in money from abroad, and jobs that don't need a university degree, exactly what Spain needed after the crash. Tourism is now about an eighth of Spain's entire economy. {p} And the same sun powers the country: in 2025, more than half of Spain's electricity came from renewables.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.narration: And it's not just the exchange rate. {p} Adjust for what things actually cost in each country, and Spain has been ahead of Japan every year since 2022. {p} In 2025, by about eight percent: the average Spaniard now produces about sixty thousand dollars' worth a year, at those prices. {pp} In 1990, by that same measure, Japan was about half again as rich.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · unemployment, youth (% of labor force ages 15–24, modeled ILO estimate), 2025
shots.title: Youth unemployment, 2025
shots.narration: But don't feel sorry for Japan just yet. {p} Look at young people looking for work. {p} In Spain, about one in four can't find a job. {pp} In Japan, about one in twenty-five. {p} A young Spaniard is more than six times as likely to be unemployed. {p} Japan has the opposite problem: it can't find enough workers.

shots.src: Japan Ministry of Finance via Jiji/Nippon.com (26 May 2026): net external assets ¥561.75 trillion at end-2025, third after Germany and China
shots.title: What Japan owns abroad, net
shots.narration: And Japan is sitting on a mountain of savings. {p} Japanese families, companies and the government own about five hundred and sixty trillion yen more abroad than foreigners own in Japan. {p} That's about three point seven trillion dollars, a record, and the third biggest pile on Earth, after Germany and China. {pp} Interest and dividends from all of it flow home every year, and a weak yen makes them worth more in yen.

And here's the uncomfortable math for Spain. {p} If the yen went back to where it was in 2019, about a hundred and ten to the dollar, Japan would jump straight back ahead, by more than ten thousand dollars a person. {p} Japan's overall unemployment is about two and a half percent. Spain's is four times that. And both countries live about as long as anyone on Earth: around eighty-four years. {pp} <soft>Spain's lead is real, but it's fragile.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · population aged 65+ (% of total) · fertility rate (births per woman)
shots.narration: And Spain faces Japan's problem, just later. {p} Spanish women now have about one point one children on average. That's even fewer than in Japan. {p} People sixty-five and over are now more than a fifth of Spain's population. {p} That's where Japan was around 2007. Today it's at thirty percent, and the share of Japanese of working age has fallen from sixty-eight percent in 2000 to under fifty-nine. {pp} Without immigrants, Spain would already be shrinking. {p} South Korea and Italy are on the same road, and Korea is moving down it fastest of all.

So is Spain really richer than Japan? {p} In dollars, yes, for now. Adjusted for prices, yes, by a little. {p} In jobs, savings and security, Japan is still far ahead. {p} But Spain did something Japan hasn't managed in thirty years: it turned a disaster into a decade of growth. {pp} <soft>The race is close, and it's no longer one-sided.</soft> {p} And for Japan, the lesson runs the other way: a country can be rich in savings and still lose ground, when its people, and its currency, shrink.
Spain isn't the only one. Poland passed Japan too, and almost nobody noticed. To see how, watch this next. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: In 2012, Japan Was 74% Richer Than Spain. Now Spain Is Ahead.
yt.description:
In 2012 the average Japanese produced about $49,600 a year and the average Spaniard about $28,500. In 2024 Spain passed Japan in GDP per person in dollars, for the first time in World Bank records going back to 1960, and in 2025 it pulled further ahead. Two reasons: the yen lost almost half its value, and Spain came back from 26% unemployment with immigration, tourism and the fastest growth among Europe's big economies. The twist: young Spaniards are six times as likely to be jobless as young Japanese, Japan sits on $3.7 trillion of net savings abroad, and a stronger yen would flip the ranking back.
